summary: Defines the Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol, connecting IPv6 hosts and routers across IPv4 networks. It treats the IPv4 network as an IPv6 link layer similar to NBMA. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5214.

plainLanguage.summary: Using the old internet roads as pretend cables for the new internet. ISATAP lets new computers talk over old roads inside one site automatically.

questions: how does isatap address configuration work
what is a potential router list
subtitle: Automatic IPv6 tunneling over IPv4 networks within an organization.

tldr.problem: Organizations have IPv4 networks but want to run IPv6. Manual tunneling is cumbersome and does not work for nodes that do not know each other in advance.
tldr.mechanism: ISATAP (Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol) treats an IPv4 network as a transparent link layer for IPv6. Dual-stack nodes embed their IPv4 address into their IPv6 interface identifier, allowing automatic tunneling and neighbor discovery without manual configuration.
tldr.outcome: ISATAP allows IPv6 hosts and routers to communicate across IPv4-only sites while the site prepares for full IPv6 deployment. It was experimental and was superseded by RFC 5214 which refines the approach.

today: RFC 4214 is Experimental. It was obsoleted by RFC 5214, which provides updated guidance and clarifications for ISATAP deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
ISATAP connects IPv6 hosts and routers across IPv4 networks without requiring global IPv6 connectivity or manual tunnel configuration. It is designed for use within a single site (an organization or campus) where nodes are dual-stack (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6).

The protocol views the IPv4 network as a link layer for IPv6 and views other nodes on the network as potential IPv6 neighbors. This means IPv6 packets are automatically tunneled inside IPv4, and neighbor discovery happens over the IPv4 network. ISATAP works whether the IPv4 addresses are globally unique or private (RFC 1918).
sections.plainLanguage: ISATAP lets new IPv6 computers talk to each other by pretending the old IPv4 network is a normal wire that connects them. No setup needed; it just works.

sections.title: ISATAP Addresses and Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
Each ISATAP node has an IPv6 interface identifier that encodes its IPv4 address. The identifier is constructed in Modified EUI-64 format: a 24-bit IANA OUI (00-00-5E), an 8-bit marker (0xFE), and the node's 32-bit IPv4 address in network byte order. This design allows routers and hosts to extract a node's IPv4 address directly from its IPv6 address.

An ISATAP node maintains a locator set: a mapping of IPv4 addresses to network interfaces, all within a single site. When a node's IPv4 address changes, the corresponding locator may be added or removed from the set. The IPv6 link-local addresses are derived from these locators, so each ISATAP interface can have multiple link-local addresses if the node has multiple IPv4 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer's IPv6 address on ISATAP contains its IPv4 address, like a name tag that says both who you are and where you live. When the address changes, the name tag is replaced.

sections.title: Automatic Tunneling and Encapsulation
sections.content:
ISATAP uses basic IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling: IPv6 packets are placed inside IPv4 datagrams with protocol number 41. The IPv4 source and destination are extracted from the corresponding IPv6 addresses. When an ISATAP node needs to send an IPv6 packet to a neighbor, it computes the neighbor's IPv4 address from the IPv6 interface identifier and encapsulates the packet.

When receiving encapsulated packets, a node checks that the packet's IPv4 source address is correct. The source address is accepted if it appears in the IPv6 source address's interface identifier, or if it is on the node's Potential Router List (the list of routers the node trusts). This validation prevents spoofing attacks from inside the site.

ISATAP interfaces also process ARP failures and ICMPv4 errors as link-layer events, treating them as signs that a path to a neighbor may have failed.
sections.plainLanguage: To send an IPv6 message to a neighbor, the computer wraps it in an IPv4 envelope using the neighbor's IPv4 address from the IPv6 label. Unwanted messages are rejected unless they come from a router the site admin approved.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery over ISATAP
sections.content:
ISATAP adapts IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) to the non-broadcast nature of the IPv4 network. Unlike a true link layer, IPv4 does not support multicast delivery across sites, so ISATAP uses unicast instead. Routers send solicited router advertisements directly to the requesting host rather than to the link as a whole.

ISATAP hosts maintain a Potential Router List (PRL): a set of IPv4 addresses of routers on the network. Hosts discover and refresh this list through manual configuration, DNS lookups (for a well-known domain like isatap.example.com), or DHCP options. The PRL helps hosts find routers and allows them to validate received router advertisements.

Hosts send router solicitations periodically to refresh their knowledge of available routers and prefixes. The interval is configurable and should be set to keep address lifetimes current before they expire.
sections.plainLanguage: Because IPv4 does not broadcast well across a site, ISATAP hosts ask routers directly for network information. The hosts keep a list of trusted routers (the PRL) and check back with them every now and then to make sure the network information is still good.

sections.title: Security and Site Administration
sections.content:
ISATAP shares the security challenges of both IPv6 and IPv4. Since packets travel through IPv4, IPv4-layer attacks are possible. However, implementing IPv6 security (IPsec or similar) is necessary even when IPv4 is secured, because IPv4 protection stops at the site boundary.

The main spoofing risk is an attacker inside the site sending false IPv6 router advertisements. The Potential Router List (PRL) limits this threat by allowing hosts to validate router advertisements. Site administrators should maintain an accurate PRL and protect the DNS domain or DHCP options that distribute it.

Site administrators should also configure IPv4 ingress filtering and protocol 41 filtering at the site border to prevent spoofed tunneled packets from outside the site.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor inside the site could pretend to be a router and trick computers. The list of real routers (PRL) helps catch this. Outside attackers are blocked by the site boundary.
